We have unknown inorganic salt, 20 mL sample. Flame test gave yellow flame. Yellow flame typical of Na+ (sodium) gives bright yellow. Also K gives lilac, Ca orange-red, Ba green, etc. So likely Na+. Could also be some other cation with yellow? Possibly Li gives crimson, not yellow. So Na+.

Now we added AgNO3, got black precipitate. Black precipitate with Ag+ indicates AgCl (white), AgBr (pale yellow), AgI (yellow), Ag2S (black), Ag2CO3 (brown), etc. Black suggests Ag2S (silver sulfide). That would indicate presence of S2- (sulfide) anion. However sample is unknown salt dissolved; if anion is S2-, the salt would be Na2S (sodium sulfide). That is plausible. But also could be AgCl? No, that's white. So black suggests sulfide.

But we need to confirm. Could also be Ag2SO3? Not typical. So likely sulfide.

We should test with acid to see H2S gas? But we have limited reagents. Could also test with Ba(NO3)2 to see precipitate. Ba2+ with sulfate gives white BaSO4. With carbonate gives white BaCO3 (but CO3-2). With sulfide gives BaS (white?). Actually BaS is soluble? Barium sulfide is soluble? Barium sulfide is soluble in water? I think BaS is soluble, but forms BaSO4 with sulfate. So not helpful.

We could test with HCl to see if H2S gas evolves (smell). Not available. Could test with acid to see if precipitate dissolves? For Ag2S, acid dissolves? Not easily.

We could also test with lead nitrate: Pb2+ with sulfide gives black PbS precipitate. So we can add Pb(NO3)2 to sample. If black precipitate forms, supports sulfide.

Let's do mix sample with Pb(NO3)2.
